readings.title: Hedgehogs crossing a village road
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Village residents saw hedgehogs near a road at dusk. A proposed sign looked helpful, but no one knew where crossings occurred most often. The main obstacle was a warning location chosen from one report. Sightings came from several streets and different seasons. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a mapped record of safe observations. Volunteers logged sightings without handling animals or entering traffic. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated one garden corridor connected two feeding areas. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced habitat guidance and a carefully placed warning sign. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: wildlife protection starts with patterns rather than guesses. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in hedgehogs crossing a village road, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: An insect garden in a public park
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A park planted flowers for pollinating insects. Visitors praised the colours but wondered why some areas were left with tall stems after flowering. The main obstacle was maintenance choices without explanation. People assumed that every dry stem signalled neglect. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used seasonal observation and visitor questions. Gardeners documented insect use and checked which signs would answer common concerns. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated standing stems provided useful shelter. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced small interpretation signs beside managed patches. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: habitat care may look different from tidy gardening. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in an insect garden in a public park, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Bird boxes on a school wall
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A school placed several bird boxes beside a playground. Few birds used them, and pupils assumed there were no birds nearby. The main obstacle was box locations selected for easy viewing. The boxes faced strong midday sun and a busy doorway. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review with qualified wildlife advisers. Staff compared locations with guidance while observing birds from a distance. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated placement mattered more than box number. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced safer sites away from disturbance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: wildlife projects should follow species needs. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in bird boxes on a school wall, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A pond visit without disturbance
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A nature reserve ran school visits to a pond. Children enjoyed looking for frogs, but groups crowded the same bank. The main obstacle was visits concentrated at one fragile edge. The route made one viewpoint easy to reach while other safe views were poorly marked. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a supervised route assessment. Rangers recorded movement and checked where visitors could see wildlife without damaging plants. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated several smaller viewing points spread pressure. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a guided loop with clear stopping places. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: education and habitat protection can support each other. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a pond visit without disturbance, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the local wildlife stewardship programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about wildlife and habitat protection, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关野生动物与栖息地保护的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the wildlife conservation team suggesting a practical change to the local wildlife stewardship programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local wildlife stewardship programme. People have noticed a warning location chosen from one report, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
